verdict_label: Contested: old insult, mixed use now
explanation: Traditionally in Greece the thumbs-up has carried a vulgar meaning similar to the middle finger, particularly when thrust abruptly or among older Greeks, and some travel-advice sources still list it as an insult to avoid. However, due to international media, texting culture, and younger generations, it is now also very commonly used and understood as plain approval — one Greek gesture guide even recommends it as a safe way to signal agreement. Because reputable sources genuinely disagree, treat this as situational rather than a flat rule.
local_tip: With older Greeks, in rural areas, or in any tense moment, skip an emphatic thumbs-up and use a nod or say 'endaxi' (okay) instead; in casual, urban, or tourist-facing settings it's normally read as plain approval.
regional_note: Older generations and more traditional or rural communities are more likely to read it as an insult than younger, urban Greeks.

also_check.note: Thumbs-up is a well-known obscene insult, roughly equivalent to the middle finger.
Thumbs-up generally reads as 'good job' or 'OK' and is a positive, low-controversy gesture.
Thumbs-up is a universally positive, uncontroversial sign of approval.
